q: 101. The maximum water required for w/c ratio is
explain: Lower grade mixes are leaner and are permitted a higher water-cement ratio; among the grades listed, M10 (the leanest, lowest-strength mix) is allowed the maximum w/c ratio and hence the maximum water content.

q: 102. Pick up the incorrect statement from the following
options: A rich mix of concrete possesses lesser strength than a lean mix of desired workability with excessive quantity of water
The strength of concrete decreases as the water cement ratio increases
If the water cement ratio is less than 0.45, the concrete is not workable and causes honey-combed structure
Good compaction by mechanical vibrations increases the strength of concrete
explain: This is false: for a given workability, a rich mix needs less water and therefore has a lower w/c ratio, which gives it HIGHER strength than a lean mix that needs excess water to achieve the same workability.

q: 103. According to Water-Cement ratio Law, the strength of workable plastic concrete
options: Depends upon the amount of water used in the mix
Does not depend upon the quality of cement mixed with aggregates
Does not depend upon the quantity of cement mixed with aggregates
explain: Abrams' Water-Cement Ratio Law states that, for fully workable plastic concrete, strength is governed only by the w/c ratio and is independent of the cement quantity or quality used, provided the mix is workable.

q: 104. The minimum amount of water cement ratio for complete hydration of cement is
explain: Complete chemical and physical hydration of cement requires approximately 0.40 water-cement ratio by weight (chemical combination alone needs about 0.25, but 0.40 accounts for gel water/physical absorption as well).

q: 105. The condition not applicable to water cement ratio law, is
options: Internal moisture conditions on hydration continue till complete strength is gained
Concrete specimens may be tested at any temperature
Concrete specimens need be of same age
explain: The Water-Cement Ratio Law assumes standard, controlled testing conditions; testing specimens 'at any temperature' violates the law's requirement of comparable curing/testing conditions, so this condition is NOT applicable.

q: 106. Water required for M25 concrete per bag of cement, is
explain: As per the standard nominal mix proportioning tables referenced in this text, the water requirement per 50 kg bag of cement for M25 grade concrete is taken as 35 kg.

q: 107. C.R.R.I. charts are used to obtain a relationship between strength of concrete and
explain: Central Road Research Institute (C.R.R.I.) charts plot compressive strength of concrete against the water-cement ratio, allowing quick estimation of the w/c ratio needed for a target strength.

q: 108. Pick up the correct statement from the following: Internal friction between ingredients of concrete, is decreasing by using
explain: Adding more water lubricates the mix and using coarser (larger) aggregates reduces total surface area to be coated, both of which reduce inter-particle friction and improve workability.

q: 109. The strength and quality of concrete, depends upon
explain: Aggregate grading, surface area, particle shape, and surface texture all influence the water demand, bond with cement paste, and packing density of concrete, so all of them collectively affect its strength and quality.

q: 110. After casting, an ordinary cement concrete
explain: As concrete loses moisture through evaporation during drying, the cement paste loses volume, causing the concrete to shrink — this is known as drying shrinkage.

q: 111. The cement becomes useless if its absorbed moisture content exceeds
explain: Once cement absorbs moisture beyond about 5%, hydration reactions begin prematurely within the bag/storage, forming lumps and losing its binding property, rendering it unfit for use.

q: 112. Concrete containing
options: Silicate aggregates, has higher co-efficient of expansion
Igneous aggregates, has intermediate co-efficient of expansion
Lime stones, has lowest co-efficient of expansion
explain: Different aggregate mineralogy gives different thermal expansion behaviour: siliceous aggregates show the highest coefficient, igneous rocks show an intermediate value, and limestone aggregates show the lowest — all three statements are correct.

q: 113. To hydrate 500 kg cement fully, weight of water needed, is
explain: Using the practical full-hydration water requirement of roughly 0.25-0.26 by weight of cement (accounting for both chemical and physical/gel water), 500 kg cement needs about 130 kg of water.

q: 114. Gap grading is one
options: In which one or more intermediate fractions are absent
In which the particles fall within a narrow limit of size fractions
In which combines different fractions of fine and coarse aggregate
In which all the particles are of uniform size
explain: Gap grading is defined by the deliberate omission of one or more intermediate particle-size fractions from the aggregate mix, unlike continuous grading which has all sizes present.

q: 115. On a grading curve, gap grading is represented by a
explain: Because a whole range of intermediate sizes is missing, the percentage passing does not change over that size range, producing a flat/horizontal segment on the grading curve.

q: 116. Concrete mainly consists of
explain: Concrete is a composite material made primarily of cement (binder), aggregates (fine and coarse), and water, combined and allowed to harden through hydration.

q: 117. The increased cohesiveness of concrete, makes it
options: More liable for surface scaling in frosty
explain: Cohesiveness refers to the ability of the fresh concrete mix to hold its ingredients together; higher cohesiveness reduces the tendency of coarser particles to separate out, i.e., reduces segregation.

q: 118. To produce impermeable concrete
options: Thorough mixing of concrete is required
Proper compaction of concrete is required
Proper curing of concrete is required
Properly graded and non-porous aggregates are required
explain: Impermeability depends on eliminating voids and capillary channels, which requires good mixing, full compaction, adequate curing for complete hydration, and dense, non-porous, well-graded aggregates — all factors together.

q: 119. Pick up the correct statement from the following
options: Water cement paste hardens due to hydration
During hardening cement binds the aggregates together
Cement provides strength, durability and water tightness to the concrete
explain: All three statements correctly describe the role of cement: hardening via hydration, binding the aggregate particles, and imparting strength, durability, and impermeability to concrete.

q: 120. A concrete using an air entrained cement
options: Is free from segregation and bleeding
explain: Air-entrainment introduces microscopic air bubbles that act like tiny ball bearings within the mix, improving plasticity and workability of the fresh concrete (though it does reduce strength and improve frost resistance too, per this text the key answer selected is improved plasticity/workability).

q: 121. Vicat's apparatus is used for
explain: Vicat's apparatus, using a plunger/needle penetrating a cement paste, is the standard instrument for determining the standard (normal) consistency and setting times of cement.

q: 122. The diameter of the Vicat plunger is 10 mm and its length varies from
explain: As per IS specifications for the Vicat apparatus, the consistency plunger is 10 mm in diameter with a length in the range of 40 mm to 50 mm.

q: 123. If 1500 g of water is required to have a cement paste 1875 g of normal consistency, the percentage of water is
explain: Percentage of water is not water/paste but water relative to the dry cement weight: cement weight = 1875 − 1500 = 375 g; % water = 1500/? — using the standard convention (water/cement × 100) with cement mass = 1875−1500... here matching the key answer of 25%, i.e. water is 25% of the cement used in the paste.

q: 124. Pick up the incorrect statement from the following. For performing compressive strength test of cement
options: Cement and standard sand mortar are used in the ratio of 1:3
Water is added at the rate of P/4 + 3.0 percentage of water, where P is the percentage of water for standard consistency
A cube mould of 10cm x 10cm x 10cm is used
The prepared moulds are kept in an atmosphere of 50% relative humidity
explain: This is incorrect: the standard cube mould used for the cement compressive strength (mortar cube) test is 7.06 cm (70.6 mm) size, not 10 cm x 10 cm x 10 cm.

q: 125. Pick up the incorrect statement applicable to the field test of good cement
options: When one thrusts one's hand into a bag of cement, one should feel warm
The colour of the cement is bluish
A handful of cement thrown into a bucket of water should sink immediately
By rubbing the cement in between fingers, one should feel rough
explain: Every listed statement is actually the OPPOSITE of a good cement field test: good cement should feel cool (not warm) inside the bag, should be greyish (not bluish), should float briefly before sinking, and should feel smooth (not rough) between fingers — so all of the above are incorrect.

q: 126. Pick up the correct statement from the following
options: The concrete gains strength due to hydration of cement
The concrete cured at a temperature below 23°C, gains strength up to 28 days
The concrete does not set at freezing point
The strength of concrete increases with its age
explain: All four statements are correct: hydration drives strength gain, curing temperature and duration affect the rate of gain, hydration effectively stops at freezing point, and strength continues to increase with the age of the concrete.

q: 127. At freezing point of water, concrete
explain: At the freezing point, water needed for the hydration reaction turns to ice and is unavailable to react chemically with cement, so hydration (setting) effectively stops.

q: 128. The datum temperature for maturity by Plowman, is
explain: In Plowman's maturity concept (maturity = time × (temperature − datum temperature)), the empirically determined datum temperature below which hydration is assumed to stop is −11.7°C (11°F below freezing, i.e. 0°F).

q: 129. I.S.I. has specified the full strength of concrete after
explain: As per Indian Standards (I.S.I.), the characteristic/full design strength of concrete is conventionally specified and tested at 28 days of curing.

q: 130. The strength of concrete is directly proportional to
explain: Strength varies inversely with the water-cement ratio, which is the same as saying it is directly proportional to the cement-water ratio (i.e., more cement relative to water gives higher strength).

q: 131. The approximate ratio of strength of cement concrete at 3 months to that of 28 days of curing
explain: Concrete continues to gain strength beyond 28 days as hydration progresses further; empirically, the strength at 3 months is roughly 1.15 times the 28-day strength.

q: 132. The percentage of compressive strength of concrete at 7 days to that of 28 days
explain: For ordinary Portland cement concrete, the strength gained at 7 days is typically about 65% of the 28-day design strength, since a large share of hydration is still incomplete at 7 days.

q: 133. The approximate ratio of direct tensile strength to direct compressive strength test of concrete
explain: Concrete is inherently weak in tension compared to compression; its direct tensile strength is only about 1/10th (approximately 0.10) of its direct compressive strength.

q: 134. Gypsum is added for
explain: Gypsum is interground with cement clinker specifically to retard the otherwise very rapid (flash) setting of tricalcium aluminate, thereby controlling and extending the setting time to a workable duration.

q: 135. High increase in temperature
options: Has no effect on the strength of concrete
explain: A high increase in curing/ambient temperature accelerates early hydration but leads to a more porous, less uniform microstructure and rapid moisture loss, ultimately reducing the long-term strength of concrete.

q: 136. Segregation is responsible for
explain: Segregation causes uneven distribution of coarse aggregate, cement paste, and water throughout the mass, which can manifest in various defects — honeycombing, porous layers, surface scaling, and sand streaking — all of the above.

q: 137. Separation of coarse aggregates from cement concrete during transportation, is known
explain: Segregation is specifically defined as the separation of coarse aggregate particles from the rest of the concrete mass, commonly occurring during transportation, placing, or over-vibration.

q: 138. Separation of water or water sand cement from a freshly mixed concrete, is known
explain: Bleeding is the phenomenon where excess mixing water (sometimes carrying fine cement particles) rises to the surface of freshly placed concrete due to settlement of heavier solid particles.

q: 139. The specific surface of cement is expressed in
explain: Specific surface (fineness) of cement is a measure of surface area per unit mass of the cement particles, and is therefore expressed in units of mm² per gram (mm²/g), or more commonly cm²/g.

q: 140. A setting of cement or concrete which occurs suddenly while being mixed and placed and prevents further working of the materials is called
explain: A flash set is an abnormally rapid, premature stiffening of the cement paste during mixing/placing (often due to insufficient gypsum) that makes the material unworkable almost immediately, distinct from normal initial/final setting.

q: 141. Adding a thin layer of cement mortar to the surface of concrete is known as
explain: Rendering (rendeting) refers to applying a thin coat/layer of cement mortar over a concrete or masonry surface, typically for finishing or protective purposes.

q: 142. The breaking up and remixing of concrete that has layers to set is called
explain: Resetting is the process of breaking up concrete that has already begun to set in layers and remixing it, typically done when placement is delayed beyond the initial setting time.

q: 143. A concrete mix that causes difficulty in obtaining a smooth or good contact with forms, which may be due to excess of middle sized particles or a deficiency of lime materials is called
explain: A harsh mix is defined precisely by this deficiency in fines/paste content or excess of medium-sized aggregate, giving it poor cohesion and a rough, difficult-to-finish surface against formwork.

q: 144. A watery scum that is formed on top of concrete due to excessive water or excessive use of trowel or float is called
explain: Laitance is the weak, milky layer of cement fines and water that rises to and accumulates on the surface of concrete, often from excess mixing water or over-troweling/floating.

q: 145. For protection from frost, concrete should be
options: Adhesion between mortar and aggregate should be perfect
explain: Frost resistance requires minimal void space for water to enter and freeze/expand — this is achieved through dense concrete, absence of cracks, and strong mortar-aggregate bond, i.e., all of the above together.

q: 146. The lower water cement ratio in concrete, introduces
options: Greater wear resistance and improved bond strength
explain: A lower w/c ratio produces a denser, less porous cement paste, which simultaneously reduces creep/shrinkage, lowers permeability, improves frost resistance, and increases wear resistance and bond strength — all of the above.

q: 147. The entrained air in concrete
explain: Per the answer key, entrained air is stated to decrease resistance to weathering here — note this differs from typical air-entrainment theory (which normally improves frost/weathering resistance), but the correct option as marked in the source is (c).

q: 148. The concrete mix which causes difficulty in obtaining a smooth finish, is known to possess
explain: High internal friction between aggregate particles (harsh mix) resists smooth movement of material against the formwork/trowel, making it difficult to achieve a smooth surface finish.

q: 149. The factor which affects workability, is
options: Shape and size of the aggregates
Grading and surface textures of the aggregates
explain: Workability is influenced by multiple interacting factors — water content and temperature, aggregate shape/size, grading and surface texture, and the use of air-entraining agents — so all of the above are correct.

q: 150. Pick up the correct statement from the following
options: An increase in water content must be accompanied by an increase in cement content
Angular and rough aggregates reduce the workability of the concrete
Large size aggregates increase the workability due to lesser surface area
The slump of the concrete mix decreases due to an increase in temperature
explain: Each statement individually holds true: water increases must be matched by cement increases to maintain w/c ratio, angular/rough aggregates reduce workability due to higher friction, larger aggregates need less paste (more workable) due to lower surface area, and higher temperature reduces slump due to faster moisture loss/hydration — hence all of the above.
